summary: Defines how a Mobile IPv6 node can bootstrap a Home Agent address, home address, and IPsec associations from pre-configured credentials, instead of static setup. It addresses the split scenario from RFC 4640. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: A phone can set up its own home-base connection from a small amount of saved info.

subtitle: How a roaming Mobile IPv6 device can find its Home Agent, get a home address and set up IPsec from almost no stored configuration.

tldr.problem: A Mobile IPv6 node needs a Home Agent address, a home address and IPsec security associations before it can work, and RFC 3775 expects some or all of these to be configured by hand, which does not scale.
tldr.mechanism: The node is pre-configured only with the domain name of its mobility provider. It finds a Home Agent through a DNS lookup, sets up IPsec with IKEv2, gets or builds a home address during that exchange, and can have the Home Agent update its DNS entry.
tldr.outcome: The split scenario, where mobility service and network access are authorized by different parties, is solved, and the text says the solution also applies to other bootstrapping cases. The RFC has since been updated by RFC 8553.

sections.title: The Bootstrapping Problem
sections.content:
A Mobile IPv6 Mobile Node (MN) must know three things before service starts: the address of its Home Agent (HA), its own home address, and the cryptographic material (shared keys or certificates) needed to set up IPsec security associations with the Home Agent. RFC 3775 does not say how to get them automatically, so administrators normally configure each Mobile Node and Home Agent by hand.

The RFC points out that manual configuration does not scale as the number of Mobile Nodes grows. It defines how a node can bootstrap this information from non-topological information and security credentials pre-configured on the node. The problem itself is described in RFC 4640.
sections.eli5: A traveling phone needs three things to use its home base: the home base's address, its own home address and a secret handshake. Typing them into every phone by hand takes forever, so this RFC lets the phone work them out.

sections.title: The Split Scenario
sections.content:
The RFC separates two roles. The Access Service Authorizer (ASA) is the operator that authenticates a node for network access. The Mobility Service Authorizer (MSA) is the provider that authorizes Mobile IPv6 service. In the split scenario these are different entities. The text gives an example: an enterprise runs a Home Agent for its user, even though the user reaches the Internet through a personal hotspot account at a coffee shop.

A second split exists between the Mobility Service Provider (MSP), which runs the Home Agent, and the MSA, which checks the user. They can be the same party or different ones. A different MSP might be used when the node is far from its MSA network and is given a closer Home Agent for performance, or when the MSA has no Home Agent of its own.

Authentication can use an AAA protocol or a PKI with certificates. With IKEv2 and EAP, only the client is authenticated by EAP, so the node may still need a certificate revocation list check. Because no assumptions are made about the access network, the text says the solution could also be applied to the integrated deployment model, though not optimized for it.
sections.eli5: Imagine your school bus company is different from the company that decides you are allowed on the bus. They have to talk to each other, and this RFC explains how the pieces cooperate when they are different companies.

sections.title: Four Components and an Option
sections.content:
The problem is split into sub-problems that can be solved independently:

  • Home Agent address discovery: a new DNS SRV record is used, so the only data that must be pre-configured on the node is the domain name of the MSP. The RFC notes that the Home Agent Address Discovery in RFC 3775 needs the home network prefix pre-configured and does not let an operator spread nodes across Home Agents in different subnets.
  • IPsec security associations: set up with IKEv2 as specified in RFC 4877, authenticated either with certificates or with EAP, depending on the operator's deployment.
  • Home address assignment: normally done by the Home Agent during IKEv2, or auto-configured by the node.
  • Authorization with the MSA: since only the MSA can verify the user's credentials, the Home Agent may need to contact it, using a PKI or an AAA infrastructure. The backend protocol is out of scope.

An optional fifth part lets the node have its Fully Qualified Domain Name (FQDN) updated in the DNS with the dynamically assigned home address.
sections.eli5: The big job is cut into small jobs: find the home base, shake hands securely, get an address, get permission, and optionally tell the phone book where you live now. Each small job can be solved separately.

sections.title: Finding the Home Agent with DNS
sections.content:
Once the node has network access, it asks a DNS server about Home Agent service. It gets the DNS server address by configuration or through DHCPv6. Two lookups are defined.

In lookup by Home Agent name, the node is configured with an FQDN such as ha1.example.com and sends a query with QTYPE AAAA to get the IPv6 address.

In lookup by service name, the node asks for a DNS SRV record (RFC 2782). The service name is mip6 and the protocol name is ipv6, so the query is for _mip6._ipv6.example.com. SRV records carry preference and weight values for several Home Agents. If the chosen Home Agent does not answer the IKE_SA_INIT messages or IKEv2 authentication fails, the node SHOULD try the next one. If none respond, it SHOULD retry after a configurable time. The server is RECOMMENDED to return AAAA records in the additional data section to save a round trip.

The RFC provides no specific load-balancing mechanism, but an MSP can get coarse load balancing by updating the SRV priorities.
sections.eli5: The phone looks up the home base in a phone book (DNS). The book can list several home bases in order of preference, and if the first one does not answer, the phone tries the next.

sections.title: Getting a Home Address
sections.content:
The home address is assigned during the IKEv2 exchange. In the simple case the node asks for one with an INTERNAL_IP6_ADDRESS attribute in a Configuration Payload of the IKE_AUTH exchange, and the Home Agent allocates one and answers with a CFG_REPLY.

A node may prefer an auto-configured address, for example a Cryptographically Generated Address or a privacy address. If it has a pre-configured home prefix, it builds an address and proposes it; the Home Agent either confirms it or assigns a different one, and the node MUST use the address the Home Agent sends. Without a pre-configured prefix, the node includes the new MIP6_HOME_PREFIX attribute in its CFG_REQUEST. The Home Agent MUST answer with prefix information for one prefix on the home link, including the prefix length. The node builds an address and runs a CREATE_CHILD_SA exchange to create security associations for it.

If the deployment cannot allow auto-configuration, the Home Agent replies with a USE_ASSIGNED_HoA Notify Payload and an assigned address, which the node MUST use. If the Home Agent's proxy duplicate address detection fails, it rejects the Binding Update with status 134. The node then picks a new address and runs CREATE_CHILD_SA again, without repeating IKE_INIT and IKE_AUTH.
sections.eli5: The phone can ask the home base to hand out an address, or ask which street it lives on and make up its own house number. If the number is already taken, it just picks another.

sections.title: Registering the Home Address in DNS
sections.content:
A dynamically assigned home address makes any existing DNS entry invalid, so the node becomes unreachable by name unless the DNS is updated. Having every node share a security association with the MSP's DNS servers would be cumbersome, so the RFC RECOMMENDS that the Home Agent perform the update. The node MAY include the new DNS Update mobility option, with flag R not set, in its Binding Update. The Home Agent MUST then update the DNS using the FQDN in the option and the address in the Home Address Option, using dynamic DNS update (RFC 2136), and MUST send a Binding Acknowledgement carrying the result.

If the FQDN belongs to the MSA, the Home Agent may have no security association with that DNS server. It then sends the FQDN and home address pair to the MSA's AAA server, which performs the update. The Home Agent still updates the reverse entry in the MSP's DNS.

To remove a stale entry, the node sends a Binding Update with the DNS Update option and flag R set. If there is no explicit removal, the Home Agent MAY use binding cache entry expiry as the trigger. To let the Home Agent check the node may use the FQDN, the node MUST use that FQDN as its IKE_AUTH identity (IDi).
sections.eli5: When you move to a new house number, the phone book still lists the old one. The home base calls the phone book to fix your entry, and removes it when you are gone.

sections.title: The DNS Update Option and Home Prefix Attribute
sections.content:
The DNS Update mobility option has type DNS-UPDATE-TYPE (17), a length field, an 8-bit Status, the R flag, a reserved field that MUST be 0, and the MN identity as an FQDN of variable length. In a Binding Update, Status MUST be 0 and is ignored. In a Binding Acknowledgement, values below 128 mean the Home Agent did the update, and values of 128 or more mean it did not.

The MIP6_HOME_PREFIX attribute (type 16) travels in IKEv2 Configuration Payloads. It holds a Prefix Lifetime (4 octets), a Home Prefix (16 octets) and a Prefix Length (1 octet). The Length field is 0 in a CFG_REQUEST and 21 in a CFG_REPLY. It carries only one prefix and is used only for home address auto-configuration, so it does not replace Mobile Prefix Discovery.
sections.eli5: These are two small forms. One says please update my name in the phone book, and the answer form says whether it worked. The other asks which street the home base is on.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
DNS is typically used without authentication, so two risks arise. A legitimate node may get a bogus Home Agent address from a bogus DNS server ("pharming"), or an attacker may get a real Home Agent address. The first is mitigated because IKEv2 requires the Home Agent to present a valid certificate before any Binding Update, so an attacker would also need a certificate the victim can verify. The second fails at IKE authentication unless the attacker has valid credentials, but the address can still be used for denial of service. The RFC says this risk is faced by any Home Agent, and lists overprovisioning, traffic monitoring and hot spares as measures. DNSSEC or TSIG/TKEY can help but are not widely deployed on end nodes.

Home agents MUST authorize each home address and MUST implement two modes: configured addresses for each node, and first-come-first-served. For dynamic DNS update, the Home Agent MUST have a security association with the DNS server, even in the same domain, and the authorization to update an FQDN MUST be checked before the update. Assigning a local or nearby Home Agent may reveal something about the node's location, so a node needing location privacy should not disclose that home address to unauthorized nodes.
sections.eli5: A trickster could give the phone a fake home base address, but the real one has to prove who it is with a secret badge. Banks of guards, spare helpers and checking IDs keep the home base from being swamped.
